rv.q: Francesca was literally and in that sense figuratively written for her, and she responds with a disciplined, detailed performance (and, obviously, torrents of beautiful singing) that answer any questions about her fitness for the part.
Bittersweet weepie though it may be at heart, this Bridges burns brightly.
The sophisticated, sumptuous score is cause for celebration.
She also confirms her position as one of the most exquisitely expressive stars in musical theater.
If there is an affair to remember here, it’s the enduring one between O’Hara and the audience.
Kelli O'Hara and Steven Pasquale, magnificently magnetic as Francesca and Robert, make the ripping feel like real heartbreak.

In other words, the love story at the center of this “Bridges,” directed with sensitive command by Bartlett Sher, gives off some bracing sparks, even if some of the plot embellishments dreamed up to broaden the musical’s scope do not feel like anything more than time-filling devices.

One of the works that put Jason Robert Brown on the map is The Last Five Years, a 2001 two-character chamber musical that deconstructs in microscopic detail the entirety of a relationship, from first encounter through marriage to breakup.
Wisely, composer/lyricist Jason Robert Brown, book writer Marsha Norman and director Bartlett Sher attempt to mitigate the book's high-flown verbiage and fantastical air.

But although Kelli O’Hara and Steven Pasquale are in glorious voice as this passionate pair, the bombastic orchestrations and Bartlett Sher’s overstated helming inflate the production into some quasi-operatic beast that thinks it’s “Aida.”

It's very well cast. Hunter Foster, as the decent but culturally limited husband, is a strong presence. But of course, it's all about the lovers. Stephen Pasquale is excellent. As a charming, troubled soul, he sings with the kind of power and conviction that leaves no doubt a new star is born.
It's richly melodic and rhythmic — and one of Broadway's best in the last decade.

'The Bridges of Madison County' had only one path to artistic success: Its two lovers had to gain the empathy - a tear, a lump in the throat - of the audience. Mission, I would definitely say, accomplished.
Ultimately, this is a chamber musical that is both introspective and modest at its core.
It’s so delightful to get caught up in her dilemma.
You enjoy the wonderful performances and the numerous soaring ballads, frustrated that this exceptional work isn't contained in a more workable musical.
She, O’Hara, and Brown make this a Bridge worth crossing, but there’s a toll of excess sentiment you’ll have to pay.
Too bad it couldn't be just that simple an evening.
Yet there are glimmers of emotional resonance and beauty in Bridges.

cn.t: Critics praise O'Hara and Pasquale's soaring vocals and Brown's lush score, but remain divided on whether the material rises above sentimental melodrama, with some finding it beautifully romantic and others calling it overwrought.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
